panels.introHtml:
Start here

Umami, cookie-free website analytics

A map of umami-software/umami 3.4.1 in C4 terms: context on the overview, the browser scripts, the Next.js server and its stores on the full map.

Umami is developed by Umami Software, Inc. and contributors under the MIT licence. This map describes it in its own words and is not affiliated with its authors.

Try it

  • Open a card to see its part of the system.
  • Play Track a page view to see how a visit is counted without cookies.
  • Click a component for what it does and where it lives in the code.
panels.overviewHtml:
The full map

One Next.js app, two kinds of traffic

Umami runs as a single Next.js process. Public, unauthenticated collection endpoints take events from tracked sites; authenticated API routes serve the dashboard, share pages and MCP clients. Both go through one query layer.

How to read it

People on the left, scripts in their browsers next, then the server opened into its components, and storage on the right. PostgreSQL is always there; ClickHouse, Kafka and Redis are optional and switched on by environment variables.

people.title: People and AI clients
people.text: Visitors of a tracked website, the site owner or team who reads the dashboard, and AI assistants that query it through MCP with an API key.

tracking.title: Track in the browser
tracking.text: Two small scripts that site owners embed: one sends page views, events and Web Vitals, the other records sessions and heatmap clicks.

ingest.title: Collect events
ingest.text: Unauthenticated routes that turn a beacon into a session and an event, without cookies: the session id is a hash of IP, user agent and a rotating salt.

app.title: Explore the data
app.text: The React dashboard and the authenticated JSON API behind it, plus the MCP endpoint that calls the same API in-process.

data.title: Store and query
data.text: One query layer picks the backend per call. PostgreSQL holds everything by default; with ClickHouse configured, analytics go there while accounts stay in PostgreSQL.

nodes.what: Someone browsing a website that embeds the Umami script, clicking a Umami short link or loading a tracking pixel.
nodes.why: Every number on the dashboard comes from these visits. Umami never sets a cookie on them; it recognises a visitor only by a hash of IP, user agent and a salt that changes every month by default.

nodes.what: Signs in, adds websites, reads traffic, builds reports and boards, invites a team, shares a public view. An admin also manages users.
nodes.why: Owners are the only ones who read data. Ownership is per user or per team, and every API call checks it.
nodes.tools: Browser on the Umami dashboard; default login admin / umami on a fresh install

nodes.what: An MCP client such as Claude or Cursor that asks questions about traffic through read-only tools.
nodes.why: Lets people ask for numbers in plain language. It authenticates with a user's API key, so it sees exactly what that user sees.
nodes.tools: Model Context Protocol over HTTP · packages/mcp/README.md lists the tools

nodes.what: A small script embedded with data-website-id. It sends a page view on load and on every pushState, clicks on elements with data-umami-event, umami.track() and umami.identify() calls, and optional Web Vitals.
nodes.why: Keeps the client side tiny and respects Do Not Track, domain lists and an opt-out flag in localStorage. It also keeps the signed cache token the server returns, so later beacons skip lookups.

nodes.what: Records DOM changes with rrweb for session replay and collects click and scroll positions for heatmaps, then sends them in batches.
nodes.why: Replays show what a visitor actually did. It reuses the tracker's session token, so it only works next to script.js.

nodes.what: The web app: websites, realtime, sessions, replays, reports (funnels, journeys, retention, goals, attribution, revenue), boards, links, pixels, teams and settings.
nodes.why: Everything the owner sees is a client-side page calling the JSON API with a bearer token, so the API is the single source of truth for the UI, scripts and MCP alike.
nodes.tools: Next.js App Router pages in src/app/(main)/ · React Query hooks in src/components/hooks/queries/ · useApi.ts · Chart.js

nodes.what: Takes every tracker beacon: validates it, drops bots and blocked IPs, derives session and visit ids, creates the session and saves the event, identify data or performance metrics.
nodes.why: This is the hot path; it must be fast and must never require a login. A signed cache token in the x-umami-cache header lets repeat beacons skip the website lookup and session insert.

nodes.what: Accepts batches of up to 200 rrweb or heatmap events (1 MB max), checks the session token and the website's recorder settings, then stores replay chunks or heatmap rows.
nodes.why: Replays are much bigger than page views, so they get their own route with a size limit and per-website switches (recorder, replay, heatmap).

nodes.what: /q/:slug looks up a short link, records a click and redirects to its URL; /p/:slug records a hit and returns a 1x1 GIF.
nodes.why: Tracks places where no script can run, such as emails and printed links. Both reuse the collect handler by calling its POST function in-process.

nodes.what: Turns the request into browser, OS, device, country, region and city, and checks the IP against IGNORE_IP (with CIDR ranges).
nodes.why: Location comes from CDN headers (Cloudflare, Vercel and others) when present, otherwise from a local GeoLite2 file, so no IP has to be stored.

nodes.what: Login with bcrypt, optional two-factor, signed tokens; reads a bearer token, API key or share token on every request and decides who may see or change a website, team, link, pixel, board or report.
nodes.why: All authorisation lives here, so the dashboard, share pages, API keys and MCP get the same rules. Tokens carry a hash of the password, so changing it logs old sessions out.

nodes.what: Read routes per website: stats, pageviews, metrics, events, sessions, realtime, replays, heatmaps and reports (funnels, journeys, retention, goals, attribution, revenue, UTM, performance).
nodes.why: Each route is thin: validate the query with zod, check permission, build filters (date range, segment, cohort), call one query function. That keeps the SQL in one place.

nodes.what: Create, update and delete users, teams, websites, links, pixels, boards, shares, segments and API keys; admin routes; share-token minting for public pages.
nodes.why: Configuration is plain CRUD over PostgreSQL through Prisma, kept apart from the analytics reads so neither depends on the other's backend.

nodes.what: A stateless MCP server over HTTP, off unless MCP_ENABLED=1. Its tools call the typed API client, whose fetch is replaced by an in-process dispatcher to an allow-list of read routes.
nodes.why: MCP never touches storage directly: every tool goes through the same route handlers and permission checks as the dashboard, with no loopback HTTP.

nodes.what: One function per question (saveEvent, getWebsiteStats, getFunnel ...). Each analytics function holds a PostgreSQL and a ClickHouse version; runQuery picks one. Account data goes through Prisma only.
nodes.why: This is what makes the store pluggable: the routes never know where analytics live. It also holds the Redis-backed loaders for websites, sessions and links.

nodes.what: Users, teams, websites, links, pixels, reports, boards, API keys and, by default, all analytics: sessions, events, event and session data, revenue, replays and heatmaps.
nodes.why: The only required dependency. Migrations run at start-up, so an upgrade is a restart. An optional read replica takes the read queries.

nodes.what: When configured, holds the analytics tables (events, event and session data, replays, heatmaps) plus materialised views that pre-aggregate per hour.
nodes.why: Column storage and hourly rollups keep dashboards fast at high volume. Accounts and configuration stay in PostgreSQL either way.

nodes.what: With ClickHouse and Kafka both set, events, event data and session links are produced to topics instead of inserted directly.
nodes.why: Buffers write bursts away from ClickHouse. Not visible in the code: what consumes the topics into ClickHouse; the repository only produces.

nodes.what: Caches website:{id}, session:{id}, link:{slug} and pixel:{slug} for 24 hours, and stores login sessions under auth:{key} when enabled.
nodes.why: Takes the website lookup off the collect hot path, and turns the login token into a revocable server-side session. SSO login needs it.

nodes.what: MaxMind's city database, downloaded at build time into geo/GeoLite2-City.mmdb and read in-process.
nodes.why: Gives country, region and city without sending the IP anywhere at runtime. Skipped when a CDN already sends location headers.

track.title: Track a page view
track.desc: A visitor opens a tracked page. The tracker sends one beacon; the server derives a cookie-free session and stores an event in PostgreSQL.

hops.t: The page loads script.js with data-website-id. Once the document is ready, the tracker sends a page view, and again on every pushState or replaceState in a single-page app.

POST /api/send with {type: 'event', payload: {website, url, referrer, title, screen, language, hostname}}. From the second beacon on, the header x-umami-cache carries the token the server returned last time.
Without a valid cache token, the website is looked up first; an unknown or deleted website gets a 400.
With Redis on, the website sits under website:{id} for 24 hours, so this lookup rarely reaches PostgreSQL.
Browser, OS and device come from the user agent; location from CDN headers if any. Bots get {beep: 'boop'} and nothing is stored; IPs in IGNORE_IP get a 403.
Otherwise the IP is looked up in the local GeoLite2 file for country, region and city.

The session id is a UUID v5 of website, IP, user agent, a salt that rotates monthly by default, and the distinct id if set. The visit id adds the start of the hour and expires after 30 idle minutes. The session row is inserted (on conflict, nothing), then the event is saved with its UTM tags, click ids and referrer.
One website_event row; custom event data also goes to event_data, and a revenue property with a currency to revenue.
The answer is {cache, sessionId, visitId}. The cache token is signed with the app secret; the tracker sends it back so later beacons skip the website lookup and session insert.

scale.title: Write at scale: ClickHouse and Kafka
scale.desc: The same beacon with CLICKHOUSE_URL set. Sessions become columns on each event, and Kafka can buffer the writes.

hops.t: The tracker does not know which backend runs; the beacon is identical.
With ClickHouse on, the collect route skips the session insert: browser, OS, device and location are copied onto every event row instead.
If KAFKA_URL and KAFKA_BROKER are set too, saveEvent produces the flat event to the event topic and its properties to event_data.
Something outside this repository moves the topics into ClickHouse.
hops.note: Not visible in the code: the Kafka consumer. The ClickHouse schema in this repository has no Kafka engine table.

hops.t: Without Kafka, the row is inserted straight into website_event. A materialised view rolls it into website_event_stats_hourly, which the stats queries read.

read.title: Read the dashboard
read.desc: A site owner signs in and opens a website. The page asks the analytics API for stats, which checks access and runs one aggregate query twice.

hops.t: The owner opens the dashboard; the pages are React components rendered in the browser.
Sign-in posts username and password. The password is checked with bcrypt; with two-factor on, a short-lived partial token is returned first.

With Redis, the session is stored under auth:{key} and the token only carries that key; without Redis the token itself carries the user id. Either way it includes a hash of the password, so a password change ends old sessions.
useWebsiteStatsQuery calls GET /api/websites/:id/stats?startAt&endAt&filters with Authorization: Bearer.
parseRequest validates the query with zod and runs checkAuth; canViewWebsiteSection allows admins, the owner, team members, or a share token for that website.
Filters are built from the query: date range (clipped by the website's reset date), URL and session filters, segment. getWebsiteStats runs for the range and again for the comparison period.
One SQL aggregate over website_event grouped by session and visit gives pageviews, visitors, visits, bounces and total time. On ClickHouse the same function reads the hourly rollup instead.
JSON with the numbers and a comparison object; React Query caches it and the cards and chart render.

replay.title: Record a session replay
replay.desc: The recorder batches rrweb events and posts them with the tracker's session token; the server stores compressed chunks.

hops.t: recorder.js records DOM snapshots and changes with rrweb, and click and scroll positions for heatmaps.
It posts batches to /api/record with the x-umami-cache token it reads from window.umami.getSession(), so the tracker must have sent a beacon first.
Requests over 1 MB, without a valid session token, or for a website whose recorder is off are refused; in cloud mode a Business plan is required. Then the same bot and IP checks as page views.
Replay events become one chunk keyed by session, visit and chunk index; heatmap events become rows with page coordinates and scroll depth.
On PostgreSQL the chunk is gzipped into session_replay.events; on ClickHouse it is inserted into session_replay with ZSTD compression.

mcp.title: Ask an AI assistant
mcp.desc: An MCP client calls a tool. The server checks the API key and runs the same route handler the dashboard uses, in-process.

hops.t: The client posts an MCP request to /mcp with an API key as bearer token. With MCP_ENABLED unset the route answers 404.
authenticateMcpRequest accepts only API keys: the key is hashed and looked up in api_key, then its user is loaded.
A tool such as get_website_stats calls @umami/api-client, whose fetch is createInProcessFetch: it matches an allow-listed route and calls the handler directly, with no HTTP round trip.
The handler checks the API key and the website permission exactly as for the dashboard.
The same query function runs against whichever backend is configured.
The tool result goes back to the assistant as MCP JSON.

buildSteps.title: Count page views
buildSteps.text: A script that posts a beacon, an endpoint that turns it into a session and an event, and PostgreSQL to keep them.
buildSteps.decision: No cookies: the session id is a salted hash of IP and user agent, recomputed on each beacon, with a signed token as a shortcut.
buildSteps.runnable: pnpm install && pnpm build && pnpm start

buildSteps.title: A dashboard to read them
buildSteps.text: Sign-in, a JSON API per website and a React dashboard on top.
buildSteps.decision: Every read goes through the same API and permission checks, so share pages and API keys come almost for free.

buildSteps.title: Cache the hot lookups
buildSteps.text: Redis for websites, sessions and links, and for server-side login sessions.
buildSteps.decision: Optional: every caller checks redis.enabled and falls back to the database.

buildSteps.title: Links and pixels
buildSteps.text: Track clicks on short links and opens of a 1x1 image.
buildSteps.decision: They call the collect handler in-process instead of duplicating its logic.

buildSteps.title: Scale the analytics store
buildSteps.text: ClickHouse for events and rollups, Kafka to buffer writes.
buildSteps.decision: Each query function carries both SQL dialects and runQuery picks one from the environment.

buildSteps.title: Replays and heatmaps
buildSteps.text: A second script and endpoint for rrweb sessions and click maps.
buildSteps.decision: A separate route with its own size cap and per-website switches, so heavy payloads stay off the page-view path.

buildSteps.title: Answer AI assistants
buildSteps.text: An MCP endpoint with read-only tools.
buildSteps.decision: Tools go through the typed API client and the existing handlers, never to storage directly.

tour.title: Analytics without cookies
body: Umami counts visits to websites that embed its script and shows them to the site owner, without cookies and without sending data to third parties.
It is one Next.js app: public endpoints collect events, an authenticated API serves the dashboard, and a query layer writes to PostgreSQL or ClickHouse.
tour.why: Knowing that collection and reporting share one process and one query layer explains most of the code layout.

tour.title: The beacon
body: Follow a page view from the tracker to the collect endpoint.
tour.why: The payload is small and carries no identifier: the server works out who the visitor is.

tour.title: Who is this, without a cookie?
body: Filter bots, find the location, hash a session id, store the event.
tour.why: The monthly salt means the same visitor becomes a new session next month by design; that is the privacy trade-off.

tour.title: Rows and a token back
body: The event lands in PostgreSQL and the tracker gets a signed token for the next beacon.
tour.why: The token is a cache, not an identity: losing it only costs an extra lookup.

tour.title: From login to a stats card
body: Sign in, then one API call per card, each checked against ownership and team membership.
tour.why: The same handlers serve share pages and API keys, so access rules are written once.

tour.title: The same API for AI assistants
body: MCP tools reach the analytics routes in-process, with an API key.
tour.why: No new data path to secure: MCP can only do what its key's user can do in the dashboard.

tour.title: When PostgreSQL is not enough
body: Set CLICKHOUSE_URL and the same functions write and read ClickHouse, optionally through Kafka.
tour.why: Swapping backends is configuration, not a fork, because each query carries both dialects.

tour.title: The whole of Umami, on one map

recap.people: Visitors are counted; owners and AI assistants read.
recap.tracking: Two scripts send page views, events and replays.
recap.ingest: Public endpoints turn beacons into sessions and events.
recap.app: Dashboard, API and MCP share one auth and permission layer.
recap.data: One query layer over PostgreSQL, or ClickHouse with Kafka, plus Redis.

body: A tracker, a collect endpoint, an authenticated API and a query layer with two backends.
The design choice that shapes everything: no cookies, so identity is a salted hash computed on the server.

collect.title: Inside the collect endpoint
collect.sub: What POST /api/send does with one beacon, in order. Early exits answer without storing anything.
collect.cap: The same handler serves page views, custom events, identify calls and Web Vitals; short links and pixels call it in-process too.

steps.d: zod schema: type is event, identify or performance; exactly one of website, link or pixel; event names may not start like a spreadsheet formula.
A signed token from the previous beacon carries website, session and visit ids.
Only when there is no valid token; Redis first if enabled.
Browser, OS, device and location from headers or GeoLite2.
UUID v5 of source, IP, user agent, rotating salt and distinct id.
PostgreSQL only, and only without a token or when the session drifted.
New visit after 30 minutes without a beacon.
Parse URL and referrer, read UTM tags and click ids, pick the event type, call saveEvent.
identify: link the session to the distinct id and save session properties.

queries.title: Inside the query layer: saveEvent
queries.sub: How one query function serves two backends. Every analytics read and write in src/queries/sql/ follows this shape.
queries.cap: Account data (users, teams, websites) never goes through runQuery: it lives in PostgreSQL through Prisma whatever the analytics backend.

steps.d: CLICKHOUSE_URL set means ClickHouse; a postgresql URL otherwise means Prisma.
Every string truncated to its column length.
Only when the data has revenue above 0 and a currency.
Session columns (browser, country, ...) are copied onto the event.

postgres.title: Inside PostgreSQL
postgres.sub: The tables the flows touch, from prisma/schema.prisma. Relations are enforced by Prisma, not by foreign keys.
postgres.cap: There is no visitor table: a visitor is a session_id derived from a hash, and a visit is a visit_id inside it. Users, websites, teams, links and pixels are soft-deleted through deleted_at.

tables.name: user
tables.note: Accounts; role user, view-only or admin.

tables.name: website
tables.note: A tracked site, owned by a user or a team.

tables.name: session
tables.note: One per derived session id; device and location stored once.

tables.name: website_event
tables.note: One row per page view, event, link or pixel hit, or Web Vitals sample.

fields.note: page view, custom, link, pixel, performance

tables.name: event_data
tables.note: Custom event properties, one row per key.

clickhouse.title: Inside ClickHouse
clickhouse.sub: The analytics tables when ClickHouse is on, from db/clickhouse/schema.sql.
clickhouse.cap: No session table: session columns are denormalised onto every event row. Dashboards read a pre-aggregated hourly table filled by a materialised view, not the raw events.

tables.name: website_event
tables.note: Raw events, partitioned by month, ordered by hour, website, session, visit.

tables.name: website_event_stats_hourly
tables.note: AggregatingMergeTree, one row per session, visit and hour.

tables.name: session_replay
tables.note: Replay chunks, compressed by the column codec.
